name: Unifiram
lead: Unifiram (DM-232) is an experimental compound that showed antiamnesic effects in animal studies, with far greater potency than piracetam [1][2]. It was developed by Italian academic researchers and is the parent of sunifiram (DM-235) [1][2]. It is not patented and is sold online as a nootropic, in the absence of human or long-term toxicity studies [1][3].

People who discuss it do so in the context of focus and mental drive for training and study. On T Nation one poster, comparing nasal dianabol with other nootropics, ranked sunifiram, unifiram and noopept as the most potent [8]. The appearance link, as users frame it, runs through concentration and motivation: better focus and learning could support more consistent training and routines. No study has tested unifiram for that purpose.
Published research consists of rodent and in-vitro pharmacology from the group that discovered it, chemistry papers on analogues and enantiomers, and review articles about nootropics [2][4][5][6][7].

paras: The medicinal chemist who led the work describes unifiram and sunifiram as two very potent molecules from his former academic group's 15 years of research on cognition enhancers, disclosed in 2000 and not protected by a patent [3]. About 12 years later he found dozens of websites offering both as drugs to improve cognition in healthy people, although only a few preclinical studies existed and long-term toxicity was unknown [3]. His review frames this as a story of academic and industrial shortcomings [3].

Early papers examined structure-activity relationships of the two molecules and a series of analogues [7]. Wikipedia notes that as of 2015 no formal human studies had been carried out, and that its sale online proceeds despite that gap [1]. A 2022 review of smart drugs in healthy individuals lists unifiram analogues among the cognitive enhancers popular with students and workers [5].

Unifiram and sunifiram showed no affinity for tested receptors, channels or transporters up to 1 micromolar and did not potentiate recombinant AMPA receptors, but both prevented amnesia caused by the AMPA antagonist NBQX in a mouse passive-avoidance test [1][4]. A review describes them as four orders of magnitude more potent than piracetam, able to prevent amnesia induced by several neurotransmitter systems and to increase acetylcholine release from rat cortex; unifiram also increased field potentials in rat hippocampal slices [2].

Wikipedia summarizes the screening results as no meaningful affinity at glutamate, GABA, serotonin, dopamine, adrenergic, histamine, acetylcholine or opioid receptors at concentrations up to 1 micromolar, and states that the exact mechanism is unknown, with indirect or downstream AMPA receptor involvement suggested by the NBQX result [1]. In mice, it also shortened pentobarbital-induced hypnosis without impairing motor coordination [1].
Unifiram is a pyrrolopyrazine derivative containing a 4-fluorophenyl sulfonyl group, with the formula C13H15FN2O3S and a molar mass of about 298 g/mol [1].

The (R)-(+) enantiomer is the more active, eliciting comparable effects at 3- to 10-fold lower doses than the (S)-(-) form in passive-avoidance and social-learning tests [1][6]. Structure-activity studies of analogues found none as potent as the parents, and identified compounds with the opposite, amnesic effect and others with analgesic activity in a rat neuropathic pain model [7].

A later series of analogues built on a tetrahydropyrazino-isoindolone scaffold, or on 1,4-diaminocyclohexane or 1,4-diaminobenzene rings, was tested in the mouse passive-avoidance test; some showed antiamnesic activity with higher potency than piracetam, while some cyclohexane derivatives induced amnesia [9].

No studies found. Published work is limited to animal and in-vitro research [2][4], and a 2022 review of nootropics in healthy individuals covers the category, including unifiram analogues. It reports that cognitive enhancers are generally perceived by users as effective, but that efficacy in healthy people is uncertain, reported improvements are temporary, and stimulant-type enhancers may carry cardiovascular, neurological and psychiatric risks [5].
Unifiram is unscheduled and sold online as a research chemical [1][3]. It appears in forum discussions of cognitive enhancers alongside sunifiram and noopept [8].

The discoverer's 2016 review frames the compounds' arrival on the web as a story of academic and industrial shortcomings, noting they were not patented [3]. Unifiram is generally unscheduled, and sellers describe it as a research chemical [1][3].

timeline.event: Unifiram and sunifiram disclosed by an Italian academic group, without patent protection [3].
Study links the antiamnesic effect of DM 232 and DM 235 to AMPA receptor pathways [4].
CNS Drug Reviews pharmacological characterization published [2].
Discoverer reviews how the compounds reached online vendors [3].

lore.intro: Unifiram is mentioned in T Nation threads as a very potent nootropic, usually in passing [8].

claims.claim: Unifiram is among the most potent nootropics
claims.believers: A T Nation poster placed sunifiram, unifiram and noopept at the top of potency [8].
claims.experts: Animal studies report potency far above piracetam [2], and its discoverer notes human and long-term toxicity data are absent [3].

card.summary: An unapproved animal-tested nootropic with no human studies and no appearance evidence.
card.note: No human or long-term toxicity data.

quick.overview:
Unifiram is an experimental nootropic from Italian labs, sold online. Sunifiram is derived from it.

No source links it to appearance.
quick.mechanism: Mechanism unknown; indirect AMPA pathway involvement has been suggested.
quick.risks: No human or long-term toxicity studies exist.

chain: Reported to enhance learning and memory in rodents
Users seek sharper focus and drive
More consistent training, study and routines supporting physique and presentation
angle.text: Unifiram is discussed as a nootropic rather than an appearance compound. The link users draw is concentration and motivation that could support regular training and self-care routines; no human study has tested it for that purpose [8].
